Analise o(s) documento(s) de cenário do projeto e gere o SRS completo no formato especificado, seguindo o processo de trabalho: buscas dedicadas na base de conhecimento para cada tipo de artefato, rastreabilidade validada entre os artefatos.

Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 6.pdf ---
SLCCI (Sea Level Climate Change Initiative)
So here's the deal — this is part of a bigger ESA effort, the Climate Change Initiative,
where they're trying to finally make proper use of thirty-plus years of Earth observation
archives instead of letting all that satellite data just sit there. There are about eleven of
these projects running in parallel, each one looking at a different climate variable, and ours
is the sea level one. Basically the science side has already been doing the heavy lifting —
building the algorithms, validating them, running a kind of prototype production setup —
and now we're at the point where somebody needs to take that prototype and turn it into
something that actually runs operationally, day in day out, and can be handed over to the
people who need the data.
What I picture happening is a system that pulls in altimetry data from a bunch of different
satellite missions, runs it through calibration and validation, cross-calibrates between
missions so everything is consistent, and spits out two kinds of products: one is like a
per-mission track of measurements, and the other is a merged, gridded product that blends
all the missions together into one consistent climate record. On top of that there needs to
be a proper archive, because reprocessing is going to happen again and again as
algorithms improve or new calibration methods come out, so we can't afford to lose the
baseline data or any of the intermediate stuff along the way.
The people using this thing day-to-day are going to be on two very different sides.
Internally you've got the folks who actually run and maintain the production line —
scientists who get pulled in when something needs deeper validation or when a new
product has to be defined, people who just judge and sign off on product quality, people
who handle the catalog and metadata, and then the more operational crowd who monitor
the system, handle incidents, deal with user requests, that sort of thing. Externally, the
audience is really the climate research community — people doing climate modelling work
who just want reliable, well-documented sea level data they can trust and build on. We're
not building this for the general public or commercial customers, it's a fairly specialized
research crowd.
One thing I want to be upfront about: we don't need to worry about near-real-time delivery.
There's a whole separate world of oceanographic services that care about getting data out
within hours for things like operational forecasting, and that's just not us — we're purely
about delayed-time and the long, reprocessed historical series for climate purposes, so
anything geared at that fast-turnaround NRT use case can be dropped from consideration
entirely. Similarly, all that formal IT service management process stuff, incident ticketing
frameworks and so on, isn't something we need to bring in here, it just doesn't fit how this
is going to be run.
Cost is a real concern too, this has to be something that's sustainable to operate long term,
not just a one-off build. And it has to be flexible — new satellite missions are coming online

during the life of the project and the algorithms themselves are going to keep changing as
the science matures, so whatever gets built can't be rigid, it needs to absorb new data
sources and let people swap in improved processing logic without everything falling apart.
There's also a push to not reinvent the wheel — there's existing infrastructure out there
already doing something very similar for ocean data more broadly, and wherever it makes
sense we'd rather lean on what's proven and working than build everything from a blank
page. Quality and traceability of the data matter a lot too, since the whole point is feeding
trustworthy numbers into the international climate change conversation, so whatever
comes out the other end needs solid metadata and documentation attached, not just raw
numbers.

Sistema: SLCCI Operational Production System

Resumo executivo: The SLCCI Operational Production System operationalizes the Sea Level Climate Change Initiative prototype by ingesting satellite altimetry observations, applying controlled calibration and validation processes, cross-calibrating missions, and producing traceable delayed-time sea-level climate records. It delivers per-mission along-track products and merged gridded products while preserving source, intermediate, and historical product versions. The system supports scientific quality assessment, metadata management, operational monitoring, reprocessing, and controlled dissemination to the climate research community.

Escopo: Operate a sustainable delayed-time production chain for generating, archiving, quality-controlling, cataloguing, and distributing satellite-derived sea-level climate products.
  Em escopo: Ingestion of altimetry datasets from multiple satellite missions
  Em escopo: Calibration and validation of mission data
  Em escopo: Cross-calibration between satellite missions
  Em escopo: Generation of per-mission along-track products
  Em escopo: Generation of merged gridded sea-level products
  Em escopo: Version-controlled reprocessing with updated algorithms or calibrations
  Em escopo: Archiving of source, intermediate, and product datasets
  Em escopo: Scientific quality assessment and product approval
  Em escopo: Metadata, provenance, and documentation management
  Em escopo: Cataloguing, search, and download of approved products
  Em escopo: Production monitoring and failed-job recovery
  Em escopo: Configuration of new missions and processing algorithms
  Em escopo: Reuse or integration of suitable existing ocean-data infrastructure
  Fora de escopo: Near-real-time data delivery — the initiative only addresses delayed-time climate products
  Fora de escopo: Operational ocean forecasting — handled by separate oceanographic services
  Fora de escopo: Products intended for the general public or commercial customers — the target audience is the climate research community
  Fora de escopo: Formal IT service management and incident-ticketing frameworks — explicitly excluded from the operating model
  Fora de escopo: Scientific development of new altimetry algorithms — algorithms are supplied and validated by scientific teams
  Fora de escopo: Processing of climate variables other than sea level — covered by other Climate Change Initiative projects
  Premissa: PA-01: Satellite missions or their data providers will supply accessible delayed-time altimetry datasets.
  Premissa: PA-02: Scientific teams will provide validated algorithms, calibration parameters, and scientific acceptance tolerances.
  Premissa: PA-03: Quality assessors will be available to review products before dissemination.
  Premissa: PA-04: [INFERRED] Existing ocean-data infrastructure will expose interfaces or components suitable for reuse.
  Premissa: PA-05: [INFERRED] Long-term storage capacity will be provisioned according to approved retention and cost plans.
  Premissa: PA-06: [INFERRED] Climate researchers will have network access and compatible scientific tools for using distributed products.
  Restrição: REST-01 (Operational): Processing and dissemination must use a delayed-time operating model.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Scope): Near-real-time processing capabilities must not be included.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Process): A formal IT service management or incident-ticketing framework must not be required.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Economic): Annual operation must remain within the approved long-term operational budget [TBD].
  Restrição: REST-05 (Technical): Suitable proven ocean-data infrastructure must be reused where technically and economically feasible.
  Restrição: REST-06 (Scientific): Released products must conform to scientific validation and quality-approval rules.
  Restrição: REST-07 (Evolution): The architecture must accommodate new satellite missions and algorithm versions.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - ESA Climate Change Initiative Sponsor (Stakeholder externo): Sustainable operations, trustworthy climate records, controlled costs, and alignment with Climate Change Initiative objectives.
  STK-02 - Production Operator (Usuário primário): Execute and monitor production and reprocessing jobs, diagnose failures, and recover interrupted processing.
  STK-03 - Sea-Level Scientist (Usuário primário): Configure scientific processing, introduce validated algorithms, investigate anomalies, and define new products.
  STK-04 - Product Quality Assessor (Usuário primário): Review validation evidence and approve or reject product releases.
  STK-05 - Catalog and Metadata Manager (Usuário primário): Maintain searchable catalog records, metadata, provenance, and product documentation.
  STK-06 - Operations and User Support Staff (Usuário secundário): Observe operational status, investigate service issues, and support specialist users without a formal ITSM framework.
  STK-07 - Climate Researcher and Climate Modeller (Usuário primário): Find, evaluate, and download reliable, documented, traceable sea-level climate products.
  STK-08 - Existing Ocean-Data Infrastructure Provider (Stakeholder externo): Receive compatible integration requests and preserve the operational integrity of reused infrastructure.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Delayed-time processing: Sea-level climate products are produced from delayed-time observations and historical reprocessing rather than near-real-time data streams.
  RN-002 - Required product families: The initiative delivers per-mission along-track measurements and a merged gridded climate record.
  RN-003 - Cross-mission consistency: Measurements from different satellite missions must be cross-calibrated before they contribute to a merged climate record.
  RN-004 - Input integrity validation: A mission dataset must satisfy the defined completeness, format, and integrity controls before scientific processing.
  RN-005 - Quality approval before release: A product may be disseminated only after an authorized quality assessor records an approval decision.
  RN-006 - Preservation of production data: Source baseline data and intermediate processing results must be retained to support traceability and future reprocessing.
  RN-007 - Immutable processing versions: Reprocessing creates a distinguishable product version and must not overwrite an existing historical version.
  RN-008 - Mandatory provenance and documentation: Every distributable product must include metadata, processing provenance, quality status, and supporting documentation.
  RN-009 - Specialist research audience: Distributed products are intended for climate researchers and climate-modelling activities rather than general-public or commercial services.
  RN-010 - Controlled scientific evolution: A new mission or algorithm version may enter operational production only after its configuration and scientific validation have been approved [INFERRED].

Requisitos funcionais:

  RF-004 - Validate processed measurements: The system must evaluate processed measurements against the scientific validation checks associated with the selected processing configuration. [Must have]
  RF-005 - Cross-calibrate missions: The system must cross-calibrate measurements from eligible satellite missions using the selected scientific configuration. [Must have]
  RF-006 - Generate along-track product: The system must generate a versioned per-mission along-track sea-level product from successfully processed measurements. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Generate merged gridded product: The system must generate a versioned gridded sea-level product from eligible cross-calibrated mission measurements. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Archive source data: The system must archive each accepted source dataset without altering its accepted baseline content. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Archive intermediate results: The system must archive the intermediate results designated by the active retention policy. [Must have]
  RF-010 - Archive product versions: The system must archive each generated product as an immutable version. [Must have]

  RF-012 - Manage catalog metadata: The system must allow an authorized metadata manager to create and update catalog metadata for a product version. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Associate product documentation: The system must associate version-specific scientific and user documentation with each distributable product. [Must have]
  RF-014 - Submit product for assessment: The system must submit a generated product version and its validation evidence for quality assessment. [Must have]

  CA-020 - Dado a production job and at least one configured operational recipient, quando the job enters the failed state, então the system sends a notification containing the job identifier, failed stage, timestamp, and error identifier within 5 minutes [TBD]
  CA-021 - Dado a failed job with a valid recovery point, quando an authorized operator requests restart, então the system creates a linked recovery execution beginning at that recovery point without altering the failed execution record
  CA-022 - Dado complete interface, validation, calibration, and metadata definitions for a new mission, quando an authorized scientist saves the configuration, então the system assigns a unique version and records its eligibility status
  CA-023 - Dado a valid algorithm package with complete dependencies and documentation, quando an authorized scientist registers the package, então the system stores it under a unique immutable version and records its validation status

Glossário:
  SLCCI: Sea Level Climate Change Initiative, the sea-level project within ESA's Climate Change Initiative.
  Altimetry data: Satellite observations used to derive sea-surface height and related sea-level measurements.
  Delayed-time: Processing performed after observations and required auxiliary information are available, without near-real-time delivery obligations.
  Near-real-time: Rapid processing and delivery within hours of observation for operational forecasting; excluded from this system.
  Along-track product: A product containing geolocated sea-level measurements organized along the observation track of an individual satellite mission.
  Merged gridded product: A spatially gridded sea-level climate record produced by combining eligible cross-calibrated observations from multiple missions.
  Calibration: Application of corrections and parameters intended to align measurements with approved scientific references.
  Cross-calibration: Adjustment and comparison of observations from multiple missions to create a consistent combined record.
  Validation: Evaluation of data or products against defined scientific checks, reference datasets, and acceptance tolerances.
  Reprocessing: Regeneration of historical products using a specified version of algorithms, calibration configurations, and source datasets.
  Baseline data: Accepted source data preserved without alteration as the foundation for processing and reproducibility.
  Intermediate result: A retained dataset produced between source ingestion and final product generation.
  Provenance: Traceability information identifying the sources, configurations, algorithms, executions, and decisions that produced a data product.
  Product version: An immutable identified instance of a product generated from a specific processing configuration and source-data selection.
  Quality assessor: An authorized specialist responsible for reviewing evidence and recording product approval or rejection.
  Climate record: A consistent long-term observational dataset suitable for climate analysis and modelling.
  Recovery point: A validated persisted processing state from which an interrupted or failed job can resume.

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.
Cadeia de rastreabilidade mínima:
STK → (RN →) RF → HU → CA

4.1 DoRCU Methodology
DoRCU, according to Griselda Báez & Barba Brunner ( 2001), has been developed in an 
academic environment and validated in a project during a public health context in Cuba. It is 
called DoRCU for Documentation of User-Centered Requirements. The article presents the 
following characteristics (Griselda Báez & Barba Brunner, 2001): (i) it consists of 4 stages: 
elicitation, analysis, specification and validation and certification of requirements; (ii) it describes 
an iterative process; (iii) it involves high user participation in all its stages; (iv) it prioritizes the 
satisfaction of user needs; and (v) it is adaptable to other models (flexibility). Fig. 2 shows a 
representation of DoRCU based on its proposal.

User personas
To help bring your user classes to life, consider creating a persona for each one, a description of a 
representative member of the user class (Cooper 2004; Leffingwell 2011). A persona is a description 
of a hypothetical, generic person who serves as a stand-in for a group of users having similar 
characteristics and needs. You can use personas to help you understand the requirements and to 
design the user experience to best meet the needs of specific user communities.
A persona can serve as a placeholder when the BA doesn’t have an actual user representative 
at hand. Rather than having progress come to a halt, the BA can envision a persona performing 
a particular task or try to assess what the persona’s preferences would be, thereby drafting a 
requirements starting point to be confirmed when an actual user is available. Persona details for a 
commercial customer include social and demographic characteristics and behaviors, preferences, 
annoyances, and similar information. Make sure the personas you create truly are representative of 
their user class, based on market, demographic, and ethnographic research.

The voiceless user class
A business analyst at Humongous Insurance was delighted that an influential user, Rebecca, 
agreed to serve as product champion for the new claims processing system. Rebecca had many 
ideas about the system features and user interface design. Thrilled to have the guidance of an 
expert, the development team happily complied with her requests. After delivery, though, they 
were shocked to receive many complaints about how hard the system was to use.
Rebecca was a power user. She specified usability requirements that were great for experts, 
but the 90 percent of users who weren’t experts found the system unintuitive and difficult to 
learn. The BA didn’t recognize that the claims processing system had at least two user classes. 
The large group of non–power users was disenfranchised in the requirements and user interface 
design processes. Humongous paid the price in an expensive redesign. The BA should have 
engaged at least one more product champion to represent the large class of nonexpert users.
Selling the product champion idea
Expect to encounter resistance when you propose the idea of having product champions on your 
projects. “The users are too busy.” “Management wants to make the decisions.” “They’ll slow us down.” 
“We can’t afford it.” “They’ll run amok and scope will explode.” “I don’t know what I’m supposed to 
do as a product champion.” Some users won’t want to cooperate on a project that will make them 
change how they work or might even threaten their jobs. Managers are sometimes reluctant to 
delegate authority for requirements to ordinary users.
Separating business requirements from user requirements alleviates some of these discomforts. As 
an actual user, the product champion makes decisions at the user requirements level within the scope 
boundaries imposed by the business requirements. The management sponsor retains the authority 
to make decisions that affect the product vision, project scope, business-related priorities, schedule, 
or budget. Documenting and negotiating each product champion’s role and responsibilities give 
candidate champions a comfort level about what they’re being asked to do. Remind management 
that a product champion is a key contributor who can help the project achieve its business objectives.

Connecting with user representatives
Every kind of project—corporate information systems, commercial applications, embedded systems, 
websites, contracted software—needs suitable representatives to provide the voice of the user. These 
users should be involved throughout the development life cycle, not just in an isolated requirements 
phase at the beginning of the project. Each user class needs someone to speak for it.
It’s easiest to gain access to actual users when you’re developing applications for deployment 
within your own company. If you’re developing commercial software, you might engage people 
from your beta-testing or early-release sites to provide requirements input much earlier in the 
development process. (See the “External product champions” section later in this chapter). Consider 
setting up focus groups of current users of your products or your competitors’ products. Instead of 
just guessing at what your users might want, ask some of them.
One company asked a focus group to perform certain tasks with various digital cameras and 
computers. The results indicated that the company’s camera software took too long to perform the 
most common operation because of a design decision that was made to accommodate less likely 
scenarios as well. The company changed their next camera to reduce customer complaints about speed.
Be sure that the focus group represents the kinds of users whose needs should drive your product 
development. Include both expert and less experienced customers. If your focus group represents 
only early adopters or blue-sky thinkers, you might end up with many sophisticated and technically 
difficult requirements that few customers find useful.

Customer involvement is the best way to avoid the expectation gap described in Chapter 2, 
“Requirements from the customer’s perspective,” a mismatch between the product that customers 
expect to receive and what developers build. It’s not enough simply to ask a few customers or their 
manager what they want once or twice and then start coding. If developers build exactly what 
customers initially request, they’ll probably have to build it again because customers often don’t 
know what they really need. In addition, the BAs might not be talking to the right people or asking 
the right questions.
The features that users present as their “wants” don’t necessarily equate to the functionality they 
need to perform their tasks with the new product. To gain a more accurate view of user needs, the 
business analyst must collect a wide range of user input, analyze and clarify it, and specify just what 
needs to be built to let users do their jobs. The BA has the lead responsibility for recording the new 
system’s necessary capabilities and properties and for communicating that information to other 
stakeholders. This is an iterative process that takes time. If you don’t invest the time to achieve this 
shared understanding—this common vision of the intended product—the certain outcomes are 
rework, missed deadlines, cost overruns, and customer dissatisfaction.
User classes
People often talk about “the user” for a software system as though all users belong to a monolithic 
group with similar characteristics and needs. In reality, most products of any size appeal to a diversity 
of users with different expectations and goals. Rather than thinking of “the user” in singular, spend 
some time identifying the multiple user classes and their roles and privileges for your product.

Expected challenges
The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are

■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good

Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement

Imagine that you’ve been asked to implement some new functionality in region A in this figure. 
Begin by recording the new requirements in a structured SRS or in a requirements management tool. 
When you add the new functionality, you’ll have to figure out how it interfaces to or fits in with the 
existing system. The bridges in Figure 21-2 between region A and your current system represent these 
interfaces. This analysis provides insight into the white portion of the current system, region B. In 
addition to the requirements for region A, this insight is the new knowledge you need to capture.CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 399

Rarely do you need to document the entire existing system. Focus detailed requirements efforts 
on the changes needed to meet the business objectives. If you’re replacing a system, start by 
documenting the areas prioritized as most important to achieve the business objectives or those that 
pose the highest implementation risk. Any new requirements identified during the gap analysis will 
need to be specified at the same level of precision and using the same techniques as you would for a 
new system.
Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.
I worked with one team that was just beginning to develop the requirements for version 2 of 
a major product with embedded software. They hadn’t done a good job on the requirements for 
version 1, which was currently being implemented. The lead BA wondered, “Is it worth going back 
to improve the SRS for version 1?” The company anticipated that this product line would be a major 
revenue generator for at least 10 years. They also planned to reuse some of the core requirements 
in several spin-off products. In this case, it made sense to improve the requirements documentation 
for version 1 because it was the foundation for all subsequent development work in this product line.

Most of this book describes requirements development as though you are beginning a new software 
or system development project, sometimes called a green-field project. However, many organizations 
devote much of their effort to enhancing or replacing existing information systems or building 
new releases of established commercial products. Most of the practices described in this book are 
appropriate for enhancement and replacement projects. This chapter provides specific suggestions as 
to which practices are most relevant and how to use them.
An enhancement project is one in which new capabilities are added to an existing system. 
Enhancement projects might also involve correcting defects, adding new reports, and modifying 
functionality to comply with revised business rules or needs.
A replacement (or reengineering) project replaces an existing application with a new custom-built 
system, a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) system, or a hybrid of those. Replacement projects are 
most commonly implemented to improve performance, cut costs (such as maintenance costs or 
license fees), take advantage of modern technologies, or meet regulatory requirements. If your 
replacement project will involve a COTS solution, the guidance presented in Chapter 22, “Packaged 
solution projects,” will also be helpful.
Replacement and enhancement projects face some particular requirements issues. The original 
developers who held all the critical information in their heads might be long gone. It’s tempting to 
claim that a small enhancement doesn’t warrant writing any requirements. Developers might believe 
that they don’t need detailed requirements if they are replacing an existing system’s functionality.

replacing an existing system to improve its ability to meet the organization’s current business needs.

2 BACKGROUND
This section briefly describes ISO 29148 emphasizing the suggested process items with which 
the axes of analysis are established and presents the relevant aspects of RE and the UC 
paradigm.
2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
ISO 29148 is a systems and software engineering standard that specifies the required 
processes to determine the product requirements (including services) of systems and software 
throughout the life cycle (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018), (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148 is aligned with 
ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 standard for software life cycle processes and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 
standard for system life cycle processes (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148, in its first edition (2011), 
replaced the IEEE 830-1998, IEEE 1233-1998 and IEEE 1362-1998 standards, also related to 
requirements engineering (IEEE SA, 2011), becoming the main standard in RE by providing a 
model adaptable to different organizations (Selvyanti & Bandung, 2017). In 2018, the second 
edition was published, due to the need to adopt a framework oriented towards a more detailed C2-4
technical approach (Ward et al., 2018), and in Boyarchuk et al. (2020) the importance of having 
a structured process in RE to build a good software product is highlighted.
ISO 29148 establishes (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018): (i) a set of 3 main processes that are iteratively 
and recursively applied in the system and software life cycle (see Fig. 1); (ii) a set of 2 related 
technical processes; (iii) each main process is composed of activities with established 
objectives to achieve a correct identification and good description of requirements; (iv) a set of 4 
types of documents for requirements specification at business, stakeholder, system and 
software levels; (v) the concept of operations and System operational concept; and, (vi) 
guidelines to manage the evolution of requirements.
2.2 User-Centered Software Requirements
The user-centered software development approach (UCD), was stablished as a response to 
existing software development schemes, which in practical terms can be noted, were focused 
on the technical aspect of the software and associated hardware (De Bellis & Haapala, 1995), 
(Norman & Draper, 1987). The UCD gained some relevance with the publication of ISO 
13407:1999 Human-centred Design Processes for Interactive Systems (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017)
and after that, when the stakeholders are included into ISO 9241-210:2010 Ergonomics of 
human-system interaction - Part 210: Human-centred Design for Interactive Systems (Vidal et 
al., 2012). Finally, the latest edition of the ISO 9241-210 standard is, recently, from 2019 (IEEE 
SA, 2011). In short, as pointed out by several authors (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017), (Forbrig, 2016), 
(Nieva et al., 2016), (Wanderley et al., 2014), and the ISO 13407 standard itself (ISO, 2019), 
RE should allow to reach an understanding of the needs, attitudes, motivations and behaviors of 
users that are the basis for achieving successful products and services, with a wide margin of 
end-user satisfaction.

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The mission is active and its source interface is configured.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The dataset is validated, registered, and archived as source baseline data.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No dataset is released to scientific processing, and the failure is recorded.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects a configured mission and requests ingestion.
2. The system retrieves the available delayed-time dataset.
3. The system validates format, completeness, mandatory fields, and checksum.
4. The system registers and archives the accepted dataset.
5. The system marks the dataset as available for processing.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. No new dataset is available → the system records a no-data outcome and ends the operation.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. Validation fails → the system rejects the dataset, records the failed controls, and marks the ingestion as failed (ref. RN-004, RF-002).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authorized and the mission interface specification is available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A versioned mission configuration is registered with its eligibility status.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No active mission configuration is created.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor creates a mission configuration.
2. The actor supplies source-interface, validation, calibration, and metadata definitions.
3. The system validates configuration completeness and interface conformance.
4. The actor records the scientific validation status.
5. The system stores the versioned mission configuration.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. Scientific validation is pending → the system stores the mission as evaluation-only.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. Configuration validation fails → the system identifies each invalid or missing item and prevents activation (ref. RN-010, RF-022).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authorized and the algorithm package and validation evidence are available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The algorithm is registered as an immutable version with a defined status.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The algorithm version remains unavailable for operational processing.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor submits an algorithm package.
2. The actor supplies version, parameter, dependency, and documentation information.
3. The system validates package integrity and metadata completeness.
4. The actor assigns the approved scientific validation status.
5. The system stores the version and makes approved versions selectable.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. The algorithm is not approved → the system stores it as evaluation-only.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. Package validation fails → the system rejects registration and reports the validation errors (ref. RN-010, RF-023).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: Required source datasets and an approved processing configuration are available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A uniquely identified reprocessing job is queued or started.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects the temporal range and source datasets.
2. The actor selects approved mission, calibration, and algorithm versions.
3. The system validates configuration compatibility.
4. The system creates a new product-version identifier.
5. The system starts or queues the reprocessing job.
fluxos_alternativos: 5a. Production capacity is unavailable → the system queues the job and displays its queue position.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The configuration is incomplete or incompatible → the system reports the conflicts and prevents execution (ref. RN-007, RN-010, RF-024).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The product has completed processing and validation evidence exists.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The product status is set to pending quality assessment.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The product remains unavailable for approval and publication.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects a generated product version.
2. The system displays its validation evidence, metadata, and provenance.
3. The actor requests quality assessment.
4. The system checks submission completeness.
5. The system records the submission and marks the product as pending assessment.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The actor adds supplementary scientific notes before submitting.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. Mandatory evidence is missing → the system lists the missing evidence and rejects the submission (ref. RN-005, RF-014).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The product is pending assessment and the actor is authorized.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: An immutable approval or rejection decision is associated with the product.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor opens the pending product assessment.
2. The system presents validation evidence, metadata, provenance, and documentation.
3. The actor selects approval or rejection.
4. The actor enters a rationale.
5. The system records the decision, actor, and timestamp.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. Additional evidence is required → the actor returns the product for revision with an explanation.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. No rationale is provided → the system prevents decision submission and identifies the required field (ref. RN-005, RF-015).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: A product version exists and the actor is authorized.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Validated metadata and documentation are associated with the product version.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The previous valid metadata remains effective.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects a product version.
2. The system displays its catalog metadata and documentation.
3. The actor creates or updates the permitted metadata fields.
4. The actor associates version-specific documentation.
5. The system validates and saves the changes.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. Documentation is unchanged → the actor confirms the existing version-specific association.
fluxos_excecao: 5b. Mandatory metadata is missing → the system rejects the update and identifies each missing field (ref. RN-008, RF-012).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The product is approved and has complete metadata, provenance, and documentation.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The product is visible and downloadable through the catalog.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects an approved product version.
2. The system validates publication prerequisites.
3. The actor confirms publication.
4. The system publishes the catalog record and product package.
5. The system records the publication event.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The actor schedules publication for a future date → the system records the schedule.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. Approval or mandatory information is absent → the system prevents publication and lists the unmet prerequisites (ref. RN-005, RN-008, RF-016).

casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Matching published product versions are displayed.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor opens the product catalog.
2. The actor specifies one or more scientific search criteria.
3. The system searches published product metadata.
4. The system displays matching versions and their quality status.
5. The actor opens a product record.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. No product matches → the system displays zero results and preserves the entered criteria.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The catalog query fails → the system displays an error identifier and allows the actor to retry (ref. RF-017).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The selected product version is published.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The complete product package is transferred to the actor.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No incomplete package is represented as successfully downloaded.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor opens a published product record.
2. The system displays data, metadata, documentation, size, and checksum information.
3. The actor requests the download.
4. The system transfers the product package.
5. The system provides the package checksum.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. Multiple package formats are available → the actor selects one supported format.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. Transfer fails → the system reports the incomplete transfer and permits a new attempt (ref. RN-008, RF-018).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: At least one production or reprocessing job exists.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The actor views the current state and execution details of the selected job.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor opens the production-monitoring view.
2. The system lists active and recent jobs.
3. The actor selects a job.
4. The system displays its stage, status, start time, elapsed time, and outcome.
5. The system refreshes active-job information.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The actor filters jobs by mission, product, status, or execution period.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. Monitoring data is unavailable → the system marks the status as unknown and records the monitoring error (ref. RF-019).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: A job is failed, the actor is authorized, and a valid recovery point exists.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A recovery execution starts from the selected valid recovery point.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The failed execution and archived data remain unchanged.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor opens a failed job.
2. The system displays the failure details and available recovery point.
3. The actor requests a restart.
4. The system validates input and configuration availability.
5. The system creates a linked recovery execution and resumes processing.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. No recovery point exists → the actor may request a complete rerun.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. Required inputs or configuration versions are unavailable → the system prevents restart and identifies the missing dependencies (ref. RF-021).

Products must go through calibration, validation, and cross-calibration between missions before being considered consistent.
Reprocessing happens repeatedly as algorithms and calibration methods evolve, so baseline and intermediate data must never be lost.
The target audience is exclusively the climate research community — not the general public or commercial customers.
Near-real-time (NRT) delivery use cases are explicitly excluded — the system only serves the reprocessed/delayed-time data flow.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a scientist, I want to perform deeper validation or define new products when needed, so that scientific quality is maintained as the system evolves.
As a quality reviewer, I want to evaluate and approve products, so that only validated data is released.
As a member of the catalog/metadata team, I want to maintain the product catalog and metadata, so that the data stays discoverable and well-documented.
As a member of the operational staff, I want to monitor the system, handle incidents, and respond to user requests, so that day-to-day operations keep running.
As a climate research community member, I want to access reliable, well-documented sea level data, so that I can trust it and build my research on it.

As a system operator, I want to reprocess historical data when algorithms or calibration methods improve, without losing baseline or intermediate data, so that the climate record stays accurate over time.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Process satellite altimetry data — the system ingests data from multiple missions, calibrates and validates it, cross-calibrates between missions, and generates the per-mission and multi-mission gridded products.
Review and release product — a quality reviewer evaluates a newly generated product and approves it for release, or flags it for correction.
Reprocess historical data — an operator triggers reprocessing of archived baseline/intermediate data using an updated algorithm or calibration method, without losing prior data.
Onboard new satellite mission — an operator or scientist configures the system to ingest data from a newly available satellite mission.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given altimetry data from two or more satellite missions, when cross-calibration is performed, then the resulting measurements are consistent across missions.
Given a reprocessing run using an updated algorithm, when processing completes, then the baseline and intermediate data from previous runs remain intact and accessible.
Given a newly generated product, when a quality reviewer evaluates it, then the product is approved for release or flagged for correction.
Given a released dataset, when a climate research community member accesses it, then the dataset includes metadata and documentation sufficient to trace its origin and processing history.
Given a new satellite mission becomes available, when it is onboarded, then that mission's data is processed without requiring a rebuild of the existing processing pipelines.
